children: Europe’s energy shock points toward tighter policy Thursday. Strong US payrolls have revived the Fed too.
Euro holds before Thursday’s decision
The
pair held near $1.16 Monday, with the euro showing little movement despite a significant repricing of global interest rates.
The pair’s calm reflects competing forces: an expected European Central Bank hike this week could support the euro, while strong US employment Friday data strengthened the dollar’s yield advantage.

The ECB is widely expected to raise its deposit rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% on Thursday. That would be its second increase since June, when policymakers began responding to energy-driven inflation.
Eurozone inflation accelerated to 3.3% in August from 2.9%, driven mainly by energy. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and fuel, eased to 2.4%.
Oil complicates the ECB’s message

Brent crude approached $97 after the US and Iran attacked vessels around the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend. Shipping through the route has fallen sharply, raising the threat of prolonged disruption.
Europe imports much of its energy, making expensive oil particularly unfriendly to regional households and businesses.
The hike decision itself may be almost fully priced, meaning the euro’s larger reaction could come from Christine Lagarde’s guidance.
Hawkish outlook — language suggesting rates may rise further — could push European bond yields higher and support the euro. A cautious “one and done” message may weaken the currency.
CPI decides the dollar’s answer

Across the Atlantic, the US added 162,000 jobs in August, nearly triple the 56,000 forecast, while unemployment held at 4.1%. Traders now see roughly a 57% chance that the Federal Reserve raises rates next week.
